title: Learning to Route Languages for Multilingual Policy Optimization
claim: Standard training samples candidates in one fixed language and misses useful signal; routing across languages surfaces better candidates and higher reward.
layout: 2 stacked panels, left-to-right flow, shared input card, dotted feedback loops
description: Two stacked rows contrast GRPO (top) with LRPO (bottom). A shared stacked input card at left holds a Chinese question about a thumbs-up gesture in Greece, with an English gloss. In the top row the question goes to a robot policy model. That model fans out to several red-bordered Chinese rollouts, all saying the gesture means good. A reward model then gives each a score of 1, compared against a reference stating the gesture is offensive. In the bottom row a language router, drawn as a colored bar chart over flags (ZH, EN, ..., AR), feeds a multilingual policy model. Its rollouts are Chinese (red), English (yellow) and Arabic (green), and the Arabic one correctly says the gesture is inappropriate. The rewards are 1, 2 and 8. Dotted arrows loop back to the policy and the router. Bold titles and flags guide the eye.
caption: Comparison of GRPO and LRPO rollout process. While standard GRPO (top) is restricted to the source language, LRPO dynamically explores rollout languages during training. In this example, while Chinese and English responses provide common misconceptions about Greek etiquette, LRPO routes the query to an Arabic rollout that captures the correct cultural nuance, leading to higher reward and more accurate knowledge grounding.
abstract: Large language models~(LLMs) are trained on heterogeneous multilingual corpora, yet existing policy optimization methods often implicitly restrict each training question to a single response language or rely on a fixed dominant language for supervision. We propose language-routed policy optimization (LRPO), an online policy optimization framework that treats language as a selectable variable. LRPO elicits multilingual rollouts for each training question and integrates their relative quality into preference-based policy updates, increasing the diversity and informativeness of training signals under the fixed rollout budget. To adaptively determine which languages to explore during reinforcement learning, we introduce a trainable language router formulated as a multi-armed bandit, balancing exploration of underutilized languages with exploitation of more informative ones. Extensive experiments show that LRPO consistently improves multilingual performance, demonstrating that adaptive language routing enables effective cross-lingual knowledge exploitation for training. We release all the resources at https://github.com/Guochry/LRPO.
